A man in a linen shirt had drifted over to the booth and was waiting with the polite patience of someone who had all afternoon. Brayden began, too fast, translating in his head as he went. "Yesterday the mayor signs, signed, a housing agreement. It is about building homes for families with, uh, low incomes." He paused, hunting, and landed on a word from this week's vocabulary sheet. "Impecunious families. It means families without much money."

"Good word," the man said. "Though you might lose some of the crowd with that one."

"There is more," Brayden said, steadying. "The council, they delayed a vote on the money. The article says the delay is one month." He had not known, thirty seconds earlier, whether he could do this, and now he was doing it, and the two facts existed at once, like holding water in both hands. He pointed at the headline. "The paper says council delays vote, with no the, and present tense, because headlines do this. Headlinese. My friend taught me the word an hour ago." The man laughed, and Cara applauded once, quietly, the way you clap for something small that mattered.

The afternoon went on like that. Brayden summarised an article about a court case in which a disputed affidavit had surfaced, and he explained the word to a teenager his own age who had stopped for the free baklava and stayed for the argument about whether a signed statement counted as truth. He summarised a piece about a street artist whose murals had transfigured the underpass by the river, and he watched a woman's face change when he said the word, as if she could see the concrete blooming. Each summary was easier and none was easy. When he fumbled a verb tense, he corrected himself out loud, and no one left.

Mr. Romano came by near closing, collecting the leftover papers, and asked how it had gone. Brayden told him about the headline, the dropped words, the present tense standing in for the past. Mr. Romano nodded and said nothing else about it, which Brayden understood as the highest grade available.

He did not know whether he would sign up again next year, or whether he would ever stop hearing English through the fence of his first language, with its pickets and gaps. He knew only that the sun was lowering over the food stalls, that Cara was waving him toward the fried dough, and that his notebook was full. He closed it, tucked it under his arm, and went.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Social loafing, the drop in effort people make in groups, shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified.
story:
The clock above the bleachers showed 6:47, and Carter was still last in the sprint line, still letting his skates carve lazy arcs while Dominick and the others bent low and pushed. It wasn't that he couldn't go. In tryouts alone, back in October, he'd beaten Dave twice around the cones. But once the team existed, once he was one of twenty in a blue jersey, something in him loosened. Practices blurred together, and his legs seemed to know it before his head did.

Then Dominick got the armband. Coach handed it to him in the dressing room on a Tuesday, calling him captain, and Dominick, who kept a notebook in his bag even at parties, stood up with an idea already half-formed. "New thing," he said, taping a sheet to the whiteboard. "Sprint times. Every drill, everybody, written down with your name next to it." Beside him Dave groaned the groan of the doomed, but Dominick just tapped the paper. "Every single one."

Carter's first timed lap was ugly. Nine seconds flat, near the bottom, and worse, it was public. His name, his number, there on the sheet where anyone could read it while pretending to drink from the fountain. That night he lay on his bed with his skates drying on the floor and thought about quitting, actually quitting, just absconding from the whole enterprise, telling his mom the season was too much with midterms coming. He could imagine her nodding. Nobody would chase him. That was, in a way, the whole problem: nobody would notice one boy coasting inside a crowd of twenty.

He didn't quit. He showed up Thursday and skated the sprint like someone was hunting him, because in a sense someone now was, someone with a stopwatch and a notebook. Eight point two. Dominick read it out without comment, but Dave, wheezing beside him at the boards, said, "You've been sandbagging all season, you animal." Carter didn't argue. The number made the argument for him.

By the third week the sheet told a story nobody could ignore. Dave, who used to coast on charm and a decent slapshot, was suddenly fourth fastest. Even the quiet defensemen, the ones Carter had privately thought of as furniture, had dropped nearly a second each. The whole team's effort had jumped, and Carter found himself talking about it with Dominick while they folded the cones after practice, the rink emptied to the sound of the Zamboni warming up in the tunnel. "There's a name for it," Dominick said, pulling his gloves off with his teeth. "Social loafing. The drop in effort people make in groups. It shrinks when each member's individual contribution can be identified." He shrugged, as if embarrassed to know it. "My sister's psych textbook."

Carter turned that over on the drive home, streetlights sliding across the windshield. He liked to think of himself as a self-motivated person, someone whose effort didn't depend on a piece of paper, and the season had quietly proven otherwise. He could hold both ideas at once, though it cost him something: the times on the sheet were real, and so was the vanity underneath them. Whether he'd have found his legs without being measured, he honestly couldn't say, and the uncertainty sat in him like a loose tooth he kept testing with his tongue.

There was a harder question, too, one he'd only admitted to Dave. Ms. Becker, who taught his English class and sometimes watched the end of practice from the walkway above the rink, had once told them that the best work people do is invisible, that nobody grades a kindness. He'd thought it was perspicacity at the time, the kind of adult insight you write in a notebook and forget. Now it seemed to argue against the stopwatch, or at least against the stopwatch as a way of living. Dominick's sheet had made them faster. Whether it had made them better was a different calculation, one Carter hadn't finished, his embryonic sense of the difference still forming somewhere behind his sternum where thoughts like that seemed to live.

The last practice before playoffs, Dominick forgot the stopwatch. Genuinely forgot, left it in his dad's truck, and stood in front of the sprint line with his hands empty and an apology half out of his mouth. Carter looked down the ice at the far cones, white against the boards, and heard the Zamboni still rumbling in the tunnel like something waiting its turn. Then he planted his stick and pushed off, hard, before anyone could say whether it counted.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 2011 the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos apparently faster than light; in 2012 the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light.
story:
Julian sen... Jordan had forty minutes before fifth period and the poster board was still blank on the lab bench. "Look at this," Julianne said, holding her phone so close to his face that he had to lean back. "Some experiment in Italy measured neutrinos going faster than light. It's everywhere. Einstein was wrong, the whole thing, everything we learned is out the window." Her voice had the particular brightness it got when she believed she had caught the world changing in real time, and Jordan, who had learned to distrust that brightness, took the phone and read the article twice.

"OPERA," he said. "The experiment is called OPERA. 2011." He looked up at the clock over the door of the science classroom. The regional science symposium was Saturday, and their proposal, the one Ms. Das had already approved and submitted, was supposed to be about consensus: how a community of researchers decides something is true. They had chosen it because it sounded safe, abstract, a topic where nobody could be wrong. Julianne wanted to tear it up and write about Einstein being overthrown, which would be, she said, a much better story.

"It is a better story," Jordan admitted. "That's the problem." He handed the phone back. "One result is a headline. It's not knowledge yet." Klara, who sat at the next bench sketching the hermit crabs from the tank in the corner, an aesthete even in a lab coat, looked over. "You're both about to pontificate," she said, "and we have a deadline, so don't." She pointed her pencil at the blank board. "Some of us have actual work."

Ms. Das was at her desk grading, and Jordan knew better than to bring her a question she would answer with another question. Instead he commandeered the classroom computer and typed the experiment's name into the search bar. Julianne hovered behind him, arms folded. "You're just going to look for people confirming what you already think," she said. "That's not science either." He didn't argue, because she had a point, and because the first result was already loading.

He read for a while without speaking. The clock ticked, Klara's pencil scratched, someone at the back dropped a graduated cylinder and swore quietly. Then Jordan turned around slowly. "2012," he said. "They traced it. The result. A loose fibre-optic cable." He let that sit for a second, watching her face change by degrees, the brightness dimming into something more careful. "And other experiments measured the neutrino speeds again. Consistent with light. The neutrinos weren't faster. The cable was loose."

Julianne pulled out the chair beside him and sat down, which was a kind of surrender. "So the newspaper was wrong." "No," Jordan said. "The newspaper was early. That's different." He wrote OPERA on the corner of the poster board, then underlined it. "The system worked, kind of. Somebody published a weird result, and instead of just believing it, other people checked it. That's the whole thing. That's actually our topic. We could use this."

Klara came around the bench and read over his shoulder. "Use what, exactly? You have one example." Jordan tapped the pen against the board. "One example and a deadline," he said. "We can't survey the whole literature by Saturday." He thought of the summer he'd spent with his uncle on the coast, walking the littoral zone at low tide, turning over rocks to see what clung underneath, and how nothing under one rock told you anything until you'd turned over twenty. He didn't say that out loud. It would have sounded like a speech.

"So we present it honestly," Julianne said. "One case. We say this is how it's supposed to work, and we admit we don't know all the ways it fails." She uncapped a marker, hesitated, then wrote across the top of the board: HOW DO WE KNOW WHAT WE KNOW? Jordan watched the letters settle, still wet, still a little crooked, and began laying out the timeline with the pen: 2011, the strange result; 2012, the loose cable; the other experiments, the speeds consistent with light. Behind them the bell rang, and Klara, without looking up, slid the cap back onto the marker and said, "Forty minutes tomorrow. Bring better arguments."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
Robert turned eighteen on the fourth of October, which made the eighth of November the first Election Day he was old enough for. He had the registration card in his backpack all through seventh period, a rectangle of cardstock he kept taking out and putting back, the way you touch a phone you are not supposed to touch. Mr. Kovalenko's government class had spent two weeks on the election, and today, the day itself, Mr. Kovalenko had pushed the desks into a circle instead of their usual rows.

"Voting is habit," Mr. Kovalenko said. "Or it's nothing. You decide which this week."

Brennan, who had organized the voter registration drive in the cafeteria in September, said that first elections were when the whole shape of the electorate got decided, that if young voters stayed home the same hegemony reelected itself forever, and that he personally had registered forty-one people. Charlie said the race in their district had been decided in the primary, that the general was a formality, and that he was going to vote anyway because his mother had made him promise. Robert said nothing. Brennan had registered him too, Robert among the forty-one, clipboard balanced on a lunch tray, Robert printing his name in block letters while Brennan read out the fields.

Mr. Kovalenko asked them what a vote actually was, mechanically. Charlie said it was a preference. Brennan said it was power. Robert said, "It's a thing you hand to somebody else and then you don't get to watch what they do with it." Mr. Kovalenko looked at him for a second longer than usual but gave nothing away, and the bell rang.

Robert had until eight o'clock. Polls closed at eight; he knew this the way he knew the building codes at his uncle's shop, because his uncle had said, take the afternoon off, go before your shift, no excuses. The polling place was the community hall on Marsh Street, a spartan room with folding tables and a banner from the fall craft fair still taped above the stage. At the check-in table a poll worker asked his name and turned pages in a binder, then turned them again.

"You're not in here," she said. "Alphabetical, and there's no Robert around your street." She showed him the page, as if he might catch an error she had missed. Robert read the names. His street was there, his neighbors were there, and he was not. His card said he was registered. He could feel the clock doing what clocks do.

"There's another option," the worker said. "You can cast a provisional ballot."

"What does that mean?"

"It's for a voter whose eligibility is in question. It goes in a separate envelope, and it counts only once officials confirm you're eligible." She said it evenly, twice a week for years probably, and slid a pink envelope across the table.

Robert did not fill it out right away. He thought of Brennan's clipboard, and of his own block letters, and of the fact that he could not remember whether he had printed his middle initial. He thought of Charlie's argument that the race was already decided, and of Brennan's argument that participation was the point, and he noticed that neither argument had anything to do with the envelope, which would be counted or not counted by people he would never meet, according to a rule he had only just learned existed. He asked whether he could call anyone to check. The worker said the election office closed at six.

It was 6:40. His shift started at seven. He filled out the provisional ballot at a voting booth with a felt-tip pen that was running dry, sealed the pink envelope, signed the outside where she indicated, and got a slip with a phone number on it he could call in ten days to find out whether it had counted. His one vote was now conditional, pending, half a vote, a Schrödinger vote, he thought, and then thought that Mr. Kovalenko would say that was not how the word worked, that a ballot did not ionize into counted and uncounted states; it either was or it wasn't, and someone would find out which.

At the door a man was coming in with a folding stool to sit on during the last hour, and it was Mr. Kovalenko, wearing a poll worker badge over his coat.

"Mr. K," Robert said. "I voted."

"Good," Mr. Kovalenko said. He was setting up the stool, checking his watch against the wall clock. "Was it on the machine?"

"Provisional," Robert said. "My name wasn't in the book."

Mr. Kovalenko stopped adjusting the stool. "You registered?"

"At school. Brennan's drive."

"Then it'll be confirmed or it won't," Mr. Kovalenko said. "Call the number. Call it twice if nobody answers." He settled onto the stool and picked up the binder of names, opened it to the R's, and began, apparently, to read them, one by one, as if looking for something.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: The phrase 'There ain't no such thing as a free lunch' was popularized by its use in Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress.
story:
The gift card arrived stapled to a survey, five dollars of coffee for ten minutes of opinions, and Kason slid both across the table at Avery like a dare. "Two birds, one stone," he said. "Free lunch." Avery looked at the survey, then at the clock above the espresso machine, which she had been watching anyway because her shift ended in twelve minutes and Rania was holding two tickets to a show that started in forty.

"There ain't no such thing as a free lunch," Avery said, mostly to hear how it sounded out loud. Kason rolled his eyes the way he did when she turned ordinary decisions into physics problems. "That's such a grandfather thing to say. Where'd you even get that?"

"Ms. Suryanto," Avery said, tipping her chin toward the corner booth where the retired librarian sat every afternoon with a crossword and a single americano she nursed for hours. "She said it last week when the bank offered me a free water bottle for opening a student account. I looked it up after, because she had that smile like there was a footnote." She untied her apron as she talked, counting the facts on her fingers. "Robert Heinlein, 1966, The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress. He's the one who popularized it. The novel, I mean. The phrase went everywhere after."

"So it's fake," Kason said, clicking his pen over the survey. "It's from a sci-fi book."

"It's real, it's just newer than it sounds," Avery said. "And it's not fake either. The five dollars is real. It's just that the ten minutes is also real, and the ten minutes is the lunch." She said that and then heard it and had to sit down on the stool by the register, because something in her chest had tilted. Ten minutes for five dollars was easy math. But the same arithmetic, scaled up, had been circling her all week like a bird that wouldn't land: the summer research position at the lab, or the road trip with Rania before they both scattered to different cities. One summer. One next-best thing, given up either way. Nobody had ever phrased it to her like a price tag before.

Rania arrived at a jog, hair still wet from the pool, and leaned on the door frame. "We're going to be late. Also you look weird. What happened?"

"Nothing happened. I'm pricing things." Avery counted her tips into the jar by the register, and her hands paused over the concert ticket money, which was exactly, to the dollar, also the price of the monthly bus pass she'd been telling herself she could wait another week to buy. She laughed, a short startled sound. "I've been such a sycophant about my own plans. Complimenting them, telling them they're all great, so I never have to pick."

"That's not what that word means," Kason said.

"It's close enough." Rania pulled a face that could have meant hurry up or please choose me, and Avery felt the moment destabilize pleasantly, like a stool rocking on one leg, all the safe options suddenly uncertain. "The gap year people are virulent about gap years," she went on, talking faster now, thinking out loud, which she only did with these two. "My mom's equally virulent about not taking one. And I keep treating the trip like the free option, the one that costs nothing. But the lab is someone's next best thing that I'd be trading away. Or the trip is. That's the actual price. Not the gas money."

Ms. Suryanto, without looking up from her crossword, said, "Four letters, 'loathing.'" Her voice carried just enough. "Fourteen across."

"Virulent," Avery called back.

"Wrong number of letters, right spirit." The old woman turned a page, and Avery thought, not for the first time, that she was being graded gently her whole life by strangers who pretended not to teach.

Rania held one of the tickets out flat on her palm, and Kason, who had apparently filled out the entire survey while they talked, tore off the five-dollar coupon and set it beside the ticket so that Avery was looking at both at once. "For scale," he said. "Everything costs something. You told me that ten minutes ago, professor." The clock over the espresso machine said her shift had ended two minutes ago, and outside the window the evening had gone that particular blue that meant the show was starting soon, or the lab's reply-by email was sitting unanswered at home, or both, always both. Avery picked up the ticket, then set it down again, then picked up the coupon and held the two pieces of paper side by side like a scientist comparing samples.

"Five dollars," she said, "or my whole future. Easy."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow.
story:
Alessio's kitchen table was covered with manuscript paper, most of it blank, one sheet crowded with erasures. Joshua sat across from him with a pencil he had chewed to splinters and a melody that refused to behave. They had been at it since four o'clock, and the assignment sheet from Ms. Sutton lay between them: sixteen bars, chord changes, standard notation, due Thursday.

"The problem is bar eight," Alessio said. "Every time you end the phrase there, it sounds like the music forgot what it was doing."

"That's sort of the point," Joshua said. "I want it to feel unfinished."

"Unfinished like a mistake or unfinished like a question?"

He didn't answer, because he wasn't sure yet. He had spent the whole week thinking about it as a mistake, playing the phrase back in his head on the bus, wincing at the way it hung in the air after the fifth chord. Nothing after it. It had embarrassed him the way a sentence embarrasses you when you stop halfway through and everyone waits.

Alessio went to the piano in the living room, an upright with a water ring on the lid, provenance unknown, hauled up three flights by his older brothers one summer and never tuned since. He played Joshua's eight bars, hesitating at the ornaments, and when he reached the last chord he lifted his hands and let it sit there in the room.

Joshua listened to the silence after it. It was not empty silence. His whole body leaned toward the piano as if the next phrase were behind it and he could pull it out by leaning. "Play that again," he said. "Just the last two bars."

Alessio played them, then played them again, and on the third time Joshua put his hand on the fallboard and stopped him. "It's the five chord," he said. "I ended on five." He had read the term somewhere in the packet Ms. Sutton gave them, half cadence, and had flipped past it because it sounded like something for exams, not something a person could use. But it was a thing you could use. A half cadence ended the phrase on the five chord, and it sounded unfinished, and the unfinished sound made a listener want another phrase after it. He had stumbled into it by accident, and the accident was better than anything he had planned.

He had been intransigent about the assignment all week, insisting to his father at dinner that the melody should be complete in itself, self-contained, a closed shape. His father had shrugged and passed the salt. Now Joshua sat at Alessio's table with his erasures and thought about suturing the two halves together, the unresolved first phrase stitched to the second one, so that the wanting was the stitch. He would end bar eight on five, deliberately, and let the second phrase answer it. That would be honest. What he still could not decide was whether the answer should actually satisfy, or whether he wanted to leave the listener a little cheated, still leaning forward at the end.

He took a fresh sheet and ruled off sixteen bars. "I'm keeping bar eight the way it is," he said. Alessio, still at the piano, struck the five chord once more and held the key down until it faded on its own. "Then write me something worth waiting for," he said.

Joshua put his pencil to the staff.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
Gabrielle had spread all ten canvases across the backyard grass, weighted at the corners with stones from her mother's flowerbed, and she was trying to look at them the way a stranger would. Every piece showed hands: her grandmother's hands folding dough, her own hands holding a bus pole, the hands of the cashier at the corner store counting change so fast they blurred. She had painted them across the whole year without once saying the word theme out loud, and now the application wanted one.

"You look like you're planning a funeral," Amari said, coming through the back gate without knocking. He dropped onto the porch step and pulled his phone out. "Genesis told me to tell you the gallery wants your wall card text by Friday. Not next Friday. This one."

"Everything wants text by Friday." Gabrielle crouched beside the dough painting, straightened a stone. "The scholarship application wants an artist's statement too. Five hundred words minimum, I think. I've written the same paragraph nine times and deleted it nine times."

Amari was already scrolling. He had a habit of finding things, receipts in coat pockets, the weather two towns over, and he read now with his thumb moving fast. "Okay, so here. Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement. A short one, like fifty to a hundred words, for wall cards and things. And a longer one, five hundred to a thousand, for applications."

Gabrielle stood up. "Two versions."

"Two versions," Amari said, and turned the phone toward her so she could see the page herself. She read it twice, kneeling in the grass with her shadow falling over his screen, and felt something loosen in her chest that had been tight since Monday. She had been trying to write one sentence that could stand beside her work at a gallery and sit in a folder in an admissions office at the same time, and it could not, and it was not supposed to.

"That's why everything I wrote sounded like a deposition," she said. "Like I was testifying under oath that my work mattered. Fifty to a hundred words. I could actually do fifty words."

Amari wanted the short version first, actually. He was curating the student show at the community center and had been all month, calling venues, taping floor lines, and he needed her card text before he could lay out the wall labels. "Bring it Thursday," he said. "I'll print them that night. And Gabrielle, if you can't get it done, tell me, because I'll put the paintings up with just your name and a blank card before I'll leave them out."

"It'll be done," she said.

She sat on the porch step with a notebook and tried the short one while the light was still good. Fifty words about hands, and she kept sliding into the long one, explaining, defending, as if someone out there was ready to vilify a teenager for painting her grandmother's knuckles. She crossed out three beginnings. The fourth she kept: a few plain sentences about hands as evidence of work, of care, of everything people do without being watched. Ninety-one words when she counted them, which felt almost criminal in its smallness after a year of painting.

"It's good," Amari said, reading it over her shoulder. "It's better than good. Now do the other one."

The other one was harder, and she did it that night at the kitchen table, then printed both in the morning. The long version said more, but it also said less, somehow; in a thousand words she had room to be careful, to admit that she had started the hands by accident, that the theme had found her instead of the other way around. She was not sure that was a thing you were allowed to admit in an artist's statement. She was not sure about the order of the paintings either, or whether the bus pole one belonged at all, since it was the most hedonistic of them, all color and motion, and it argued with the quiet of the others.

Friday she carried the portfolio box to the community center, and Amari hung the paintings while she stood by the wall holding her printed card, watching him decide the height of each nail. He set the dough painting last, dead center.

"Read it to me," he said. "Before I tape it up."

Gabrielle unfolded the short statement and read it out loud in the empty gallery, her voice too loud in the room, and Amari nodded slowly, the label still in his hand.

"Okay," he said. "Now the long one. I want to hear what you didn't say."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In the recapitulation, the second theme usually returns in the home key rather than the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began.
story:
Max's kitchen smelled of burnt toast and pencil shavings, and on the table between them lay the score, open to the Andante of Mozart's Piano Sonata in F, its margins crowded with Max's handwriting and Layla's empty stares. Monday's listening quiz would decide whether Mr. Nwosu let them into the spring chamber ensemble, and Layla had gotten the first two sections right on the practice test and then fallen off a cliff.

"I can hear the exposition," she said, tapping the first page. "Tonic, theme one, then it shifts and the second theme comes in higher, in the dominant. Then development, everything gets pulled apart. That part I like. It's the recap I can't find. It all sounds the same to me after measure forty."

"That's because you're listening with your eyes half-closed." Max slid the kettle off the stove before it could shriek. "Years of choir sensitized your ear to melody, but you're ignoring the bass. The bass is where the key lives."

Layla resented how easily he said it. She had spent Sunday night with her headphones on, replaying the recording until her mother knocked on the door and asked whether something was wrong, and something was, though Layla couldn't name it. The movement wouldn't hold still for her. It moved, and moved, and ended, and she could not say where it had ended, only that the ending felt like arriving somewhere she hadn't left.

"Play it from the second theme in the exposition," she said. "Just that bit."

Max set the needle down and the phrase rose out of the speakers, bright and singable, sitting comfortably high. Layla followed it with her finger, then flipped forward, past the development, past the page where Mozart took the theme apart and recombined it like someone shuffling a deck, and stopped where the same melody reappeared near the end. She set the two passages side by side and read them together, her lips moving.

"Here," she said slowly. "The notes aren't the same."

"Of course they're not, it's the recap, he varies things."

"No, listen." She hummed the exposition phrase, then the later one, and the later one sat lower, grounded, the same tune with its feet on a different floor. She played the recording again, watching her finger track the bass under the returning melody, and the bass was home. "The second theme comes back, but it's not in the dominant anymore. It's in the key where the whole thing started. F. It comes back to F."

Max leaned over the score. The window behind him had gone dark, and in the glass their two reflections bent over the page like conspirators. "Huh," he said, and she could tell he hadn't known it either, had been bluffing about the bass all afternoon, and the discovery was suddenly hers alone, a small warm room she was standing in by herself.

"So that's how you know it's the recap," she said. "Not just because the tune comes back, but because it comes back changed in that one way. In the exposition it's in the dominant, and in the recapitulation it comes home." She copied the key signatures into her margin, then wrote the words second theme, home key beside them, pressing hard enough to dent the next page. It felt like a fact she could hold in her hand.

The kettle ticked as it cooled. Max texted Lyric, who replied with a string of exclamation marks and a complaint that the three of them were becoming an oligarchy of theory nerds running the class without her, and that Monday's quiz had better not be deleterious to her average. Layla laughed, but she was already playing the movement a third time, and this time she heard the whole shape: away, and apart, and back, the melody returning not as a repeat but as a settling, closing the circle it had opened. What she still couldn't say, even to herself, was whether Mozart had made it feel inevitable or whether she had only learned to hear it that way, whether the ending was in the music or in her. She lifted the needle and slid the record into its sleeve.

"Again," she said. "From the top."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
story:
The planning office smelled of toner and old coffee, and Ashley had claimed the back desk by the window because from there she could see the reservoir, a grey plate of water held between the hills like something the town had set down and forgotten. Her internship was supposed to be filing. On her third morning she stopped filing, because the folder in her hand had a title page that read Millbrook Water Capacity Projection, 1972, and the date alone made her curious enough to sit down and read it.

Reese had told her the internship would be boring in exactly this way. "You'll find one weird document and live inside it for six weeks," they'd said, and Ashley had laughed, and now here she was, living inside it. The memo inside the folder was a letter, typed on onionskin, from a man named as a consultant to the town council. She read it twice.

To the Council: You have asked whether Millbrook can double its housing stock by 1990. I have put your numbers through the model the MIT team built for the Club of Rome, the one published in 1972. It is called World3, and it links population, food, industry, pollution and resources, so that changing one moves the others. On your current plan, water demand passes the safe yield of the reservoir before the housing is half built. I am told this is not the answer anyone wanted. That is not my problem.

"Reese," Ashley said into her phone, wedging it against her shoulder, "what do you know about 1972?" She could hear Reese's sister's television in the background. "There was a report, apparently. For the Club of Rome. MIT team, computer model. World3, it was called. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources, all wired together. Some consultant ran our town through it." She turned the onionskin page. "Nobody wrote anything back. There's no reply in the folder. They just filed it."

The office manager, when Ashley brought the folder to her, shrugged without looking up. "That was before the big development went in. And before the second one." She signed a disbursement form for a pump contractor and slid it across the counter. "The state underwrites part of the expansion loan, so there's money to talk about, if that's what you're asking. We've always found the money." Ashley hadn't been asking about money, but she wrote it down anyway, because the sentence felt like the middle of something. She walked back to her desk past the window, and outside, past the reservoir, the cornfields on the far shore were already browning in July, their stalks shorter than the ones in the seed catalog pinned to the break-room corkboard, which advertised a drought-tolerant hybrid and described its phenotypic advantages in small confident type. She wondered whether the corn had been that hybrid, or whether the town had simply planted what it always planted.

Christophe came by at lunch because he was interning two doors down at the extension office and because he liked being fed. She gave him half her sandwich and the letter. He read it with his eyebrows going up in stages. "So the model said no," he said. "And the town said yes anyway." He tapped the page. "But look, it's just a model. Models are wrong all the time." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and Ashley found she minded it more than she expected.

"That's what I keep going around," she said. "Either they ignored it, or they were right to ignore it, and I can't tell which. The reservoir's still here. The town's still here. Nobody's died of thirst." She pointed at the window. "But the level's been dropping every summer since I learned to swim, and last August they asked us to stop watering the lawn. So the model wasn't exactly wrong. It was just slow." Christophe looked out at the water, chewing, and didn't answer, which was one of the things she liked about him.

She spent the afternoon doing what she could actually do: she photocopied the letter, printed the last ten years of reservoir levels from the monitoring database, and pinned both to the corkboard next to the seed catalog, with a note asking whether anyone in the office remembered 1972. Before she left, Mr. Yamamoto from the water district came in to drop off a report, paused at the corkboard, and stood reading the photocopy for a long moment. He was old enough that she suddenly did the arithmetic and felt her face go warm.

"You found Frank's letter," he said. He didn't look at her. "I was nineteen. I helped him punch the cards." He touched the edge of the paper as though checking it was real, then picked up his report from the counter and stood there holding it, not quite leaving. "You know what the strange part was," he said. "Everyone argued about whether the model was right. Nobody ever asked what we'd do if it was."
